newsitem.title: USA: Molybdenum demand set to outstrip supply in 1997.
newsitem.headline: Molybdenum demand set to outstrip supply in 1997.

text.p: Molybdenum demand is set to exceed supply this year, leading to a drawdown in stocks while prices will continue to fluctuate with a possible ferro-moly price spike to $16 a pound on the cards, Alice Agoos of trade publication Ryan's Notes said.

Ryan's Notes, which held a conference on vanadium, molybdenum and columbium, forecast molybdenum demand at 238 million pounds this year, with supply at 235 million pounds, leading to a 3 million draw in stocks which, by yearend would be down to 68 million pounds or 3.4 months of demand.
Data for her presentation was obtained after surveying the world's key producers, with large agreement in the industry on supply and demand projections.

Market leader Cyprus Amax was set to produce 60 million pounds this year, up from 56 million in 1996), with Kennecott at 20 million, Montana Resources at 11 million, Thompson Creek at 18 million, BHP Copper (Magma) at 5.4 million, Phelps Dodge at 2.85 million, Molycorp, a possible 8 million, Placer Dome at 14.2 million, Highland Valley at 3.5 million, Codelco at 30 million, Mexico 8.3 million, Peru 8.4 million, Chinese exports at 35 million, CIS at 4.5 million, and molybdenum recovered form catalysts at 6 million.
Stainless steel production accounts for about 31 percent of molybdenum consumption.
"Demand for molybdenum is expected to continue growing at 3 percent a year," Agoos said.
She forecast molybdenum prices remaining at $4.25 to $5.00 per pound for moly oxide and $5.00 to $6.20 for Western grade ferro-moly this year.
Moly oxide prices were expected to fluctuate by $2 to $3 per pound, with a possible spike to $16 per pound for moly oxide.
"The problem with thin pipeline stocks is that they make the market vulnerable to even small supply disruptions," Agoos said.

There may be a squeeze on Western grade ferro moly after the Chinese sold a lot of material on the market in January and February, pushing down prices so that Western converters of moly oxide into ferro moly lowered their output.

Moly pricing was also volatile because traders have such a large handle on the market, though some delegates countered that producers now have the upper hand, selling their concentrates to converters and others, and not necessarily to traders.
